comparison: Both strongly support the core finding of GABAergic-specific defects. OpenEval R3 focuses on drug hypersensitivity and genetic epistasis data (C26-C29, C31-C33), while Peer R1 encompasses broader evidence including behavioral, optogenetic, and morphological data showing E/I imbalance and GABAergic selectivity (C26-C29, C41-C53, C63, C88, C134-C135). Peer review provides more comprehensive affirmation across multiple experimental approaches.

Both support GABAergic morphological defects. OpenEval R5 evaluates quantitative synaptic puncta data (C41-C44), which is included in Peer R1's broader affirmation of GABAergic dysfunction. Peer review encompasses this finding within the larger context of E/I imbalance evidence.

Both support behavioral evidence of GABAergic dysfunction. OpenEval R6 evaluates omega turn assay data (C45-C49), which Peer R1 includes as part of the comprehensive evidence for GABAergic-specific defects and E/I imbalance.

Both support optogenetic evidence of GABAergic dysfunction. OpenEval R7 evaluates optogenetic activation data showing selective GABAergic impairment (C50-C53), which Peer R1 explicitly mentions as part of the combined pharmacological, behavioral, and optogenetic experiments demonstrating GABAergic signaling impairment.

Both support morphological defects in GABAergic neurons. OpenEval R8 evaluates detailed morphological analysis showing developmental defects (C54-C59), while Peer R3 affirms neurodevelopmental defects in GABAergic motoneurons. Both accept the developmental timing evidence distinguishing defects from degeneration (C93-C95).

Both support cell-autonomous action of DAF-18/PTEN. OpenEval R9 evaluates cell-specific rescue experiments (C60-C62), while Peer R3 affirms cell-autonomous action based on rescue data (C110). Both accept the evidence from multiple transgenic lines.

Both support developmental timing evidence. OpenEval R18 evaluates claims about defects arising before DD rewiring (C93-C95), which Peer R3 implicitly accepts by affirming neurodevelopmental (not degenerative) defects in GABAergic neurons.

Both support the conclusion about PI3K pathway hyperactivation causing GABAergic defects. OpenEval R10 evaluates summary conclusions (C63-C64), while Peer R2 affirms the mechanistic pathway involving DAF-18/PTEN acting upstream of PI3K-PDK-1-AKT-DAF-16/FOXO.

Both support genetic epistasis evidence. OpenEval R3 evaluates double mutant data showing non-additive effects (C31-C33), while Peer R2 affirms the genetic epistasis and pathway analysis demonstrating DAF-18/PTEN acts upstream of the PI3K pathway.

Both support differential effects of pathway mutations. OpenEval R4 evaluates loss-of-function vs gain-of-function pdk-1 mutations (C34-C37), while Peer R2 accepts the pathway analysis. Both support the conclusion that reduced DAF-16/FOXO activity during development causes defects (C64, C89, C104).

Both support exclusion of TOR pathway involvement. OpenEval R4 notes the inability to test certain mutants but accepts negative TOR data (C38-C40), while Peer R6 explicitly affirms the authors exclude a role for the TOR pathway based on Figure 1E data.

Both support asymmetric pathway effects. OpenEval R4 evaluates differential effects of loss-of-function vs gain-of-function mutations (C34-C37), while Peer R7 accepts that pathway exacerbation leads to E/I imbalances while pathway inhibition shows no differences, supporting the critical period hypothesis (C136-C137).

Both support DAF-16/FOXO involvement in β-hydroxybutyrate rescue. OpenEval R11 evaluates sod-3::GFP reporter data showing DAF-16-dependent effects (C65-C68), while Peer R4 strongly affirms β-hydroxybutyrate rescue is DAF-16-dependent across all experimental measures.

Both support behavioral rescue by β-hydroxybutyrate. OpenEval R12 evaluates behavioral rescue data with DAF-16 dependence (C69-C72), while Peer R4 explicitly affirms β-hydroxybutyrate partially rescues GABAergic neuron development and function in a DAF-16-dependent manner.

Both support functional rescue of E/I imbalance by β-hydroxybutyrate. OpenEval R13 evaluates optogenetic data showing bidirectional improvement (C73-C75), while Peer R4 affirms the rescue of developmental defects in morphology and function of GABAergic neurons.

Both support morphological rescue by β-hydroxybutyrate. OpenEval R14 evaluates morphological rescue data with DAF-16 dependence (C76-C78), while Peer R4 explicitly mentions rescue of proper development including morphology of GABAergic neurons.

Both support the primary conclusions about β-hydroxybutyrate rescue and DAF-16 mechanism. OpenEval R17 evaluates summary conclusions (C88-C91), while Peer R4 strongly affirms these findings as significant demonstrations of ketone body and DAF-16 importance in neurodevelopment.

Both support negative results for AIY and HSN neurons. OpenEval R15 evaluates the lack of β-hydroxybutyrate rescue in these neurons (C79-C82), while Peer R8 accepts these findings and raises questions about whether GABAergic selectivity relates to neurotransmitter class per se. Both accept the eggshell impermeability explanation.

Both strongly support the critical period findings. OpenEval R16 evaluates developmental timing experiments showing early larval requirement (C83-C87), while Peer R5 explicitly affirms rescue occurs only with early larval diet provision, supporting a critical and sensitive developmental period for DAF-18/PTEN function.

Both support the critical period interpretation. OpenEval R26 evaluates claims about developmental timing and critical periods (C124-C127), while Peer R5 affirms the developmental timing data and critical period hypothesis for DAF-18/PTEN function in GABAergic neurons.

Both support foundational background claims. OpenEval R1 evaluates literature-based context about PTEN, PI3K pathway, and neurodevelopmental disorders (C1-C3, C9-C12), while Peer R9 accepts these and other background claims as established knowledge, noting prior work on PTEN/daf-18 and daf-16/FOXO in other contexts.

Both support background claims about C. elegans as a model system. OpenEval R2 evaluates claims about C. elegans utility and pathway conservation (C13-C16), while Peer R9 accepts these contextual claims without challenge.

Both accept integrin-related speculation as reasonable hypothesis. OpenEval R19 rates claims about integrins as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct testing (C96-C99), while Peer R9 does not challenge these speculative claims, accepting them as reasonable context based on prior literature.

Both support contextual claims about neuronal selectivity. OpenEval R20 evaluates claims about selective vulnerability patterns (C100-C102), while Peer R9 accepts these contextual claims that help interpret the findings within broader patterns.

Both support the distinction from TOR-dependent mechanisms. OpenEval R21 evaluates claims about mammalian studies and pathway differences (C103-C104), while Peer R2 implicitly accepts this by affirming the DAF-16/FOXO-dependent mechanism without TOR involvement.

Both support contextual claims about PTEN and neurodevelopment. OpenEval R22 evaluates claims about PTEN's role in neuronal morphology and connectivity (C105-C111), while Peer R9 accepts these background claims, with Reviewer 3 explicitly noting prior work on PTEN/daf-18 neurodevelopmental phenotypes.

Both support translational context claims. OpenEval R23 evaluates claims about ketogenic diet clinical applications (C112-C115), while Peer R9 accepts these contextual claims that provide translational relevance for the work.

Both accept HDAC mechanism as reasonable speculation. OpenEval R24 rates HDAC-related claims as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct testing (C116-C119), while Peer R9 does not challenge these speculative mechanistic claims based on prior literature.

Both accept insulin signaling mechanism as reasonable speculation. OpenEval R25 rates claims about insulin signaling modulation as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct measurement (C120-C123), while Peer R9 accepts these as plausible mechanisms without requiring additional validation in this study.

Both accept VD neuron development speculation. OpenEval R27 rates claims about VD neuron timing as UNCERTAIN (C128-C129), while Peer R9 does not challenge these speculative claims about developmental mechanisms.

Both support the developmental model synthesis. OpenEval R28 evaluates the integrated developmental model (C130-C137), rating it as SUPPORTED with acknowledgment that direct pathway measurements would strengthen it. Peer R9 accepts the contextual background claims, while Peer R7 explicitly accepts the model (C136-C137).

Both accept translational speculation with appropriate caution. OpenEval R29 rates mammalian therapeutic extrapolation as UNCERTAIN (C138-C140), noting substantial validation would be required. Peer R9 accepts these speculative claims as reasonable future directions without requiring validation in the current study.
